vignette:
Eduardo doesn't look at his hands when he plays guitar anymore. He used to watch them move, the way his fingers found the strings without thinking, the calluses pressing into the fretboard like old friends. Now he keeps his eyes closed or stares at the ceiling, because if he looks down, he sees the flash of chrome, the wet shine of asphalt, the way his left hand looked twisted and wrong against the steering wheel.

The accident happened fourteen months ago, on a Tuesday night in late October. He'd been driving home from a gig in San Jose, the last of a three-night run. The band had played well, the crowd had been generous, and he'd felt that familiar, quiet hum of satisfaction as he merged onto the 101. It was raining-softly, just enough to make the road dark and slick. He remembers the oncoming headlights cresting the hill, remembers thinking, that car is too far over, and then the sound. A sound he still hears in the middle of the night, a deep, crumpling roar that has no beginning and no end.

The other driver had fallen asleep at the wheel, crossed the median, and hit Eduardo's sedan head-on at sixty miles per hour. Eduardo was awake for all of it. He remembers the airbag hitting his chest, the seatbelt cutting into his collarbone, the strange, quiet moment after the impact when everything was still and he could taste blood and dust in his mouth. He remembers trying to move his left hand and seeing his fingers bent at angles that made him feel sick. He remembers thinking, I'm a guitarist. I can't have this.

He spent three days in the ICU. His left hand required two surgeries to repair the fractures in his metacarpals and a torn tendon in his ring finger. His ribs were cracked, his spleen lacerated, and he had a concussion that left him with a headache for six weeks. The physical recovery took nine months. He did the hand therapy, the stretching, the painful, slow work of regaining dexterity. His fingers work now-mostly. He can play scales, he can play chords, but the speed and the fluidity he had before, the effortless muscle memory, is gone. He tells himself he's still good. He knows he's still good. But he doesn't trust his hands anymore.

What he doesn't tell his bandmates is that the real problem isn't his hand. It's the driving. It's the highway. It's the sound of rain on the roof. He can't get behind the wheel without his chest tightening, without his palms sweating, without the image of those headlights coming at him again. He takes back roads now, even for short trips to the grocery store. He avoids the 101 entirely. When he has a gig more than twenty minutes away, his wife, Mariana, drives him. She doesn't complain. She just takes the keys and says, "Vamos, mijo." She's been patient, but he sees the worry in her eyes when she catches him staring at the highway exit sign, frozen, his hand on the door handle.

The nightmares started about a month after the accident. He dreams of the impact, but it's always different. Sometimes he's in the car, but the steering wheel is made of glass. Sometimes he's playing on stage, and his fingers fall off one by one. Sometimes he's holding his guitar, and the body of it is the crumpled hood of his car. He wakes up gasping, drenched in sweat, and Mariana holds him until his breathing slows. He's started drinking more-a beer or two before bed to take the edge off, sometimes a whiskey when the images won't stop. He knows it's not a solution. He knows it makes the sleep worse. But it's the only thing that quiets the noise.

At his last gig, three weeks ago, they were playing a slow blues number. The drummer was keeping a quiet shuffle, the bass was low and warm, and Eduardo was playing a solo, his eyes closed. For a moment, it felt like before. The notes were coming, the feeling was there. And then the bass player hit a low, sustained note that rumbled through the floor, and Eduardo felt the vibration in his chest, and suddenly he wasn't on stage anymore. He was in the car, the impact was happening, and his hand was bent and wrong. He stopped playing. He stood there, guitar in hand, heart hammering, while the band played on around him. He told them he had a cramp. He doesn't think they believed him.

He hasn't scheduled another gig. He tells himself he's just taking a break. He tells Mariana he's fine. He tells his bandmates he's working on new material. But the truth is, he can't stop seeing those headlights. And he doesn't know how to play music when he's still trying to survive the moment the music stopped.
